m: This is the ritual direction for the first narrative. The seer is Brahma, the deity Mahakali, the metre Gayatri, the power Nanda, the seed Raktadantika, the element fire, and the form the Rigveda. It is recited to please Shri Mahakali. The meditation says: I serve Mahakali, three-eyed and adorned on every limb, shining like a dark-blue stone, with ten faces and ten feet, holding sword, discus, mace, arrows, bow, iron bar, spear, sling, a head, and a conch — she whom lotus-born Brahma praised, while Hari slept, so that Madhu and Kaitabha might be slain.
Om. Salutation to Chandika. Om Aim. Markandeya said:
Savarni, son of the sun, who is called the eighth Manu — hear the full account of his birth, as I tell it.
By the power of Mahamaya, that fortunate Savarni, son of the sun, became lord of a manvantara.
In the earlier age of Svarochisha there was a king named Suratha, born in the Chaitra line, ruling the whole circle of the earth.
While he protected his people as a father protects his own sons, kings who were destroyers of the Kolas became his enemies.
He, whose power to punish was very great, fought them, and those destroyers of the Kolas defeated him in battle even though they were fewer.
He then returned to his own city and remained ruler only of his own country. Those powerful enemies overran that fortunate king.
There too, in his own city, wicked and powerful ministers of evil mind took the treasury and the army from the weakened king.
His sovereignty gone, the king, on the pretext of a hunt, mounted a horse alone and went into a dense forest.
There he saw the hermitage of Medhas, foremost of the twice-born: peaceful, inhabited by wild animals, and graced by the sage's disciples.
Honoured by that sage, he stayed for some time, walking about in that excellent hermitage.
Then, his mind pulled by the sense of mine, he thought: that city, once protected by my forefathers and by me, is now without me.
I do not know whether those ill-behaved servants of mine still govern it according to dharma. And my chief war-elephant, always in rut, the brave one —
has fallen into the power of my enemies. What enjoyments will he now receive? Those who always followed me, sustained by my favour, wealth, and food —
surely now serve other kings. By those men, who spend without restraint and keep on spending —
the treasury I gathered with great pain will come to ruin. The king went on thinking of this and of other things.
Near the brahmin's hermitage he saw a merchant. The king asked him, Who are you, sir, and what brings you here?
Why do you look sorrowful, as if your mind were cast down? Hearing these affectionate words of the king,
the merchant answered him, bowing with courtesy.
The merchant said:
I am a merchant named Samadhi, born in a family of wealthy people.
My sons and my wife, dishonest and greedy for wealth, cast me out. They took my wealth, and I was left without wealth, wife, or sons.
Unhappy, and cast out by my own relatives, I came to the forest. Staying here, I do not know whether my sons are well or unwell,
nor how my own people and my wife are faring. Is their house safe now, or is it not?
How are they? Are my sons of good conduct, or of bad conduct?
The king said:
Those greedy sons, that wife, and the others cast you out for the sake of wealth.
Why does your mind still bind affection upon them?
The merchant said:
It is just as you have said about what has happened to me.
What can I do? My mind will not become hard. Those who, greedy for wealth, set aside a father's love and rejected me —
my heart still turns toward them, and toward the love one has for one's own people. I do not understand this, great-minded one, even though I know it:
that the heart stays inclined to love even toward relatives who lack virtue. Because of them I sigh, and dejection arises in me.
What am I to do, when my mind is not harsh toward those who feel no love for me?
Markandeya said:
Then the two of them together approached that sage, O brahmin.
The merchant named Samadhi and that best of kings exchanged the proper and fitting greeting with him.
The merchant and the king sat down and told one another some stories.
The king said:
Blessed one, I wish to ask you one thing. Please tell me that.
My mind suffers, though it is not under my own control. Even after the kingdom is lost, I feel mine toward every limb of the kingdom.
I know this, and still I am like one who does not know. What is this, best of sages? This man too was wronged by his sons and his wife, and left by his servants.
His own people abandoned him, and still his heart is greatly with them. So he and I are both exceedingly unhappy.
Even while seeing the fault in the thing, our minds are pulled by mine. What is this, fortunate one — this delusion even in people who understand?
This foolishness, blind to discernment, comes over me and over him.
The seer said:
Every living being has knowledge within the field of sense-objects.
And those objects, fortunate one, pass away, each in its own way. Some creatures are blind by day; others are blind by night.
Some creatures see equally by day and by night. Human beings are indeed knowing, but they are not the only knowing beings.
Cattle, birds, deer, and the rest are also knowing. The knowledge that humans have is the same knowledge that deer and birds have,
and what those have, humans also have; some of it is common to both. Even with knowledge, look at these birds, so intent on the mouths of their young,
and at the moths, who from delusion fall into the fire though hunger already torments them. Human beings, O tiger among men, are full of longing toward their children.
Out of greed, looking for a return. Do you not see this? Even so, they are thrown into the whirlpool of mine, into the pit of delusion,
by the power of Mahamaya, who keeps the world in place. There is nothing to wonder at in this. She is the yoga-sleep of the lord of the world.
She is this great illusion of Hari, and by her the world is bewildered. That blessed Goddess draws even the minds of those who know
and, by force, hands them over to delusion. By her this universe is sent forth, this world of what moves and what does not move.
When she is pleased she is the giver of boons, and for human beings she becomes the way to release. She is the supreme knowledge, eternal, the cause of liberation.
And that same sovereign of all sovereigns is also the cause of bondage in the world.
The king said:
Blessed one, who is this Goddess whom you call Mahamaya?
How did she arise, and what is her work, twice-born one? What is her power, what is her form, and what is her origin?
I wish to hear all of that from you, best of those who know Brahman.
The seer said:
She is eternal, the very form of the world. By her all this is pervaded.
Even so, hear from me the many ways her arising is told. Whenever she becomes manifest so that the work of the gods may succeed,
the world then says that she has arisen, though she is eternal. When, at the end of a kalpa, the world had become a single ocean, Vishnu
stretched out upon Shesha and the blessed Lord entered the sleep of yoga. Then two terrible asuras, known as Madhu and Kaitabha,
born from the wax of Vishnu's ears, rose up to kill Brahma. Brahma, lord of creatures, was seated on the lotus growing from Vishnu's navel.
Seeing those two fierce asuras, and seeing Janardana asleep, he praised that yoga-sleep with a one-pointed heart,
so that Hari might wake — she who makes her home in Hari's eyes. He praised the sovereign of the universe, the supporter of the world, she who brings about both continuance and dissolution,
the blessed sleep of Vishnu, whose splendour has no equal. The lord said:
Brahma said:
You are svaha. You are svadha. You are the vashat call, and you are the embodiment of the svara sounds.
You are the nectar. Eternal and imperishable, you abide as the three measures of the syllable. You abide as the half-measure, eternal, which is not pronounced as a separate sound.
You yourself are the twilight and Savitri, and you, Goddess, are the supreme mother. By you this universe is borne. By you this world is created.
By you, Goddess, it is protected, and at the end you always consume it. At creation you are the form of creation; in protection you are the form of continuance.
And at the end you are the form of dissolution of this world, O you whose being is the world. You are the great knowledge, the great illusion, the great intelligence, the great memory.
You are the great delusion, the great Goddess, the great sovereign. You are the nature of all, she who apportions the three qualities.
You are the night of time, the great night, and the terrible night of delusion. You are Shri. You are the sovereign. You are modesty. You are the understanding whose mark is awakening.
You are shame, nourishment, and contentment. You are peace, and you are forbearance. You bear the sword, the spear, the mace, and the discus, and you are terrible.
You also bear the conch, the bow, arrows, the sling, and the iron bar. You are gentle, gentler than everything gentle, and surpassingly beautiful.
You are the supreme beyond both the higher and the lower. You yourself are the supreme sovereign. Whatever thing exists anywhere, real or unreal, O self of all —
the power of every such thing is you. Why would I praise you? He by whom the world is created, he who protects the world, he who is the world —
even he has been brought under the sway of sleep. Which lord here is able to praise you? Vishnu, I myself, and Ishana
have been caused by you to take bodies. Who, then, could have the power to praise you? Goddess, you have thus been praised by these noble powers of your own.
Bewilder these two asuras, Madhu and Kaitabha, who are hard to assail. And let the lord of the world, Achyuta, be brought quickly to waking.
Let him be awakened, so that he may slay these two great asuras.
The seer said:
Praised in this way by Brahma, the Goddess whose nature is tamas, there,
in order to awaken Vishnu and to strike down Madhu and Kaitabha, came forth from his eyes, mouth, nostrils, arms, heart, and chest,
and stood within Brahma's sight, he whose birth is unmanifest. Released by her, Janardana, lord of the world, rose.
Then, from his serpent-couch on the single ocean, he saw those two, Madhu and Kaitabha, evil-minded, of exceeding strength and valour,
their eyes red with anger, intent on killing Brahma. The blessed Hari rose and fought the two of them.
For five thousand years the all-pervading one fought, his arms his weapons. Those two, exceedingly strong and intoxicated, bewildered by Mahamaya,
said to Keshava, Choose a boon from us.
The blessed Lord said:
Be pleased with me today, both of you, and let both of you be slain by me.
What use is any other boon here? This alone is what I choose.
The seer said:
Thus outwitted, and seeing that the whole world was nothing but water,
they said to the blessed lotus-eyed one: slay us where the earth is not flooded by the waters.
The seer said:
So be it, said the blessed bearer of conch, discus, and mace. With his discus he cut them on the thighs, and then severed their heads.
She arose in this way, praised by Brahma himself. Now hear further the majesty of this Goddess. I will tell it to you.
